content.text: {"relation": "MATCH", "consensus_summary": "All four blind responses converge on the same core: the image of metals in Nebuchadnezzar's dream (Daniel 2) symbolizes a succession of earthly/Gentile world empires — traditionally Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome, and a divided final phase — which are ultimately destroyed and replaced by God's everlasting kingdom, symbolized by the stone cut without hands. Disagreement among interpreters concerns only the precise identification of the later kingdoms (Rome-terminating vs. Greece-terminating schemes) and the timing of the stone's kingdom, not the basic referent.", "book_summary": "The book identifies the image of metals as 'the succession of gentile world-kingdoms, shattered by the stone-kingdom of God,' citing Daniel 2:32-45 and cross-referencing the Mountain entry.", "consensus_core_identification": "A succession of Gentile/world kingdoms or empires, decreasing in glory, destroyed and superseded by God's eternal kingdom (the stone).", "book_core_identification": "The succession of Gentile world-kingdoms, shattered by the stone-kingdom of God.", "core_relation": "EQUIVALENT", "extension_relation": "SAME_CASES", "boundary_disagreement": "None. The book's terse entry does not commit to a specific identification of the individual kingdoms (Rome-terminating vs. Greece-terminating), so it neither narrows nor broadens the consensus; it simply states the shared core on which all schemes agree.", "material_contradiction": "None. The book affirms exactly what all consensus responses affirm as the near-universal core meaning.", "rationale": "The book's identification — successive Gentile world-kingdoms destroyed by God's stone-kingdom — is verbatim the primary meaning given by all four blind responses (Response D even uses the phrase 'Gentile world empires' and Responses A-C describe the same referent). Daniel 2:36-45 itself supplies this interpretation, which is why the consensus is settled. The book declines to specify which historical empires the metals denote, but since that specification is the only locus of disagreement among interpreters and the book takes no position on it, there is no boundary or extension difference. This is a straightforward MATCH.", "citation_support": "STRONG", "strongest_objection": "One could argue the book's silence on the identity of the kingdoms (Babylon/Medo-Persia/Greece/Rome) makes it vaguer than the consensus primary meaning, and that vagueness could conceal a divergent scheme in the full chapter. However, omission of detail in a glossary line is not disagreement, and the stated core is identical to the consensus core; the cited passage explicitly supports the succession-of-kingdoms reading.", "confidence": "high"}
